about.title: About Power-to-Weight Ratio Calculator
about.description: The Power-to-Weight Ratio Calculator determines the relationship between engine power and vehicle weight for comparison and reference use. It is useful for comparing acceleration potential across different vehicles or setups. Power-to-weight ratio is commonly used to review how changes in weight or power may affect vehicle behavior.

howTo.title: How to Use the Power-to-Weight Ratio Calculator

steps.title: Enter Engine Power
steps.description: Input vehicle horsepower (HP) or kilowatts (kW) at the wheels or crank.

steps.title: Input Vehicle Weight
steps.description: Enter total vehicle weight including fuel, fluids, and driver in pounds or kilograms.

steps.title: Calculate Ratio
steps.description: View the calculated power-to-weight ratio (lbs/hp or kg/kW).

steps.title: Compare Performance
steps.description: Compare your results with performance benchmarks and vehicle categories.

tips: Use curb weight plus driver weight for accurate calculations
Lower ratios indicate better performance (more power per pound)
Consider both horsepower and torque for complete performance picture

faq.q: What's considered a good power-to-weight ratio?
faq.a: Sports cars typically achieve 6-10 lbs/hp, supercars reach 4-6 lbs/hp, and hypercars achieve under 4 lbs/hp. Economy cars usually range from 12-20 lbs/hp. Our power-to-weight calculator helps you determine where your vehicle stands in these categories.

faq.q: How does power-to-weight ratio affect acceleration?
faq.a: Lower power-to-weight ratios (more power per pound) generally correspond to stronger acceleration potential. The exact result varies with traction, gearing, aerodynamics, and drivetrain type, so power-to-weight ratio is best used as a comparison metric rather than a direct prediction.

faq.q: Is it better to add power or reduce weight for performance?
faq.a: Reducing weight is often more effective than adding power because weight reduction improves acceleration, braking, handling, and fuel economy simultaneously. Weight reduction also doesn't stress the drivetrain components like increased power output does.

faq.q: How do motorcycles compare to cars in power-to-weight ratio?
faq.a: Motorcycles typically have superior power-to-weight ratios, often achieving 2-4 lbs/hp for sport bikes compared to 6-10 lbs/hp for sports cars. This explains motorcycles' exceptional acceleration performance despite lower absolute horsepower numbers.

faq.q: Should I use crank horsepower or wheel horsepower for calculations?
faq.a: Wheel horsepower (WHP) provides more accurate real-world performance predictions since it accounts for drivetrain losses. Crank horsepower is higher but doesn't reflect actual power reaching the wheels. Our calculator works with both measurements.

faq.q: What power-to-weight ratio do I need for racing?
faq.a: Racing requirements vary by class: drag racing often uses under 8 lbs/hp, road racing commonly falls in the 6-10 lbs/hp range, and autocross setups are often below 12 lbs/hp. Check the specific rules for the series you care about.
